sections.text: What you can do with Orbit A household can use Orbit to: keep a list of the things it looks after, as services, renewals, inspections, documents that expire, and ideas to come back to; give each one a due date and say how often it comes round; get reminders before an item is due, by default 14 days and 3 days ahead; keep a document beside the item it belongs to; share all of it with the other people in the household. Orbit runs on your own server, so your household's records stay with you.

sections.title: The screens
sections.summary: The screenshots below are the real app, filled with made-up data for a made-up household. They hold no real accounts or settings.
sections.text: The screens The screenshots below are the real app, filled with made-up data for a made-up household. They hold no real accounts or settings. Your sky The home screen is "your sky": the year drawn as a dial, with your household at the centre and today at the top. Each thing you look after is a body on its own orbit. The closer it sits to the centre, the sooner it is due; overdue items sit inside the event horizon, the dashed red ring around your sun. The "key" tab on the right explains the colours and sizes. The search box at the bottom, "explore your world", finds items and documents. One item Open any body in the sky, or any row on home, and its drawer opens in place: when it is due, what section and type it is, how often it comes round, what it costs, who provides it, its reference and its reminders, then your notes and the documents attached to it, stored encrypted. Press a document and a preview stands beside the drawer; press the preview to read the whole thing. From the drawer you can snooze it, complete it, attach a document or retire it; the pencil edits it in place, picking dates from a calendar. Complete it and Orbit works out the next date for you. The inbox Everyone gets their own relay address. Forward a bill or a policy to it and the inbox shows "what your relay has caught": what Orbit read from the attachment, and whether the attachment passed the malware scan. Nothing is added until you choose "Add to orbit". Anything left unreviewed is removed after 45 days, and Orbit only ever reads copies of your mail. An administrator sets up the mailbox first: see the mailbox. Settings Settings holds your own choices: how you sign in, which of the five themes your sky uses (star-chart, after dark, clouds, dawn and retrograde; after dark is the default), when reminders arrive and whether by email or browser alert, and your relay address. "Watch the tour" replays the short tour film that Orbit offers once you have a household. Settings for the whole instance live on the administration screen instead.

sections.title: Around your household
sections.summary: Share the load. A household's owner can add people who already have an Orbit account, or send an invitation by email. Owners can also hand the household over to someone…
sections.text: Around your household Share the load. A household's owner can add people who already have an Orbit account, or send an invitation by email. Owners can also hand the household over to someone else. Sections that fit. Home, Vehicles, Devices and Services to begin with. Add, rename, reorder and recolour your own. On your phone. The main screens have their own phone layout. Orbit installs like an app and can send browser alerts. Your household's data stays on your server: the app keeps no copy of it on the phone, and changes are never saved up to send later. Private by design. Use Orbit's own accounts, or an identity provider you already run (any OpenID Connect provider, such as Authentik). Nobody sees a household without signing in. See Authentication.

sections.title: One app. Standard parts.
sections.summary: You bring a Linux machine with Docker, and an HTTPS address for it. It runs three containers: Orbit itself, the official PostgreSQL 18 image for your records, and the…
sections.text: One app. Standard parts. flowchart LR browser["Your browser or phone"] orbit["Orbit"] postgres[("PostgreSQL 18")] documents[("Encrypted documents")] scanner["ClamAV malware scanner"] optional["Optional: identity provider, email, browser alerts, mailbox"] browser <-->|HTTPS| orbit orbit <--> postgres orbit --> documents orbit -->|each upload| scanner orbit <-.-> optional You bring a Linux machine with Docker, and an HTTPS address for it. It runs three containers: Orbit itself, the official PostgreSQL 18 image for your records, and the official ClamAV image, which checks every upload before it is kept. ClamAV wants about 4 GiB of memory. An administrator can turn scanning off, and Orbit then marks later uploads as not scanned. If you like, add email reminders, browser alerts, an identity provider and the mailbox your relay forwards into. Two heavier services are also optional: a document text reader (Apache Tika) and a private AI model server (Ollama). See Running Orbit. Your data stays on your own disk: records in the database, documents encrypted with a separate key for each one. Encryption at rest says what that protects and what it does not. Updates: run the launcher again and choose Update. Every release is pinned to one exact build, and your settings carry over. See Installing Orbit.

sections.title: Join or start a household
sections.summary: When you first sign in and you are not yet in a household, Orbit asks where do you belong? You have two choices.
sections.text: Join or start a household When you first sign in and you are not yet in a household, Orbit asks where do you belong? You have two choices. Ask to join a household that already exists. Press ask to join beside its name. The row then says waiting until the household's owner approves or declines you. Start your own. Press name your own system, give it a name, choose its time zone and currency, and press Create. A new household starts with four sections: Home, Vehicles, Devices and Services. If you are already signed in but in no household, your sky says you’re adrift. Press one of the household labels in the sky to ask to join it: Orbit asks Request to join … system?, and you press request to join. If someone invited you by email, open the link in the message. Orbit asks you to sign in, then takes you straight into that household. The link only works for someone signed in with the exact address it was sent to. sections.title: Find your way around
sections.summary: Your home screen is your sky. Each thing you look after sits on the dial, and the list below it shows the same things in date order:
sections.text: Find your way around Your home screen is your sky. Each thing you look after sits on the dial, and the list below it shows the same things in date order: anything overdue first, then a TODAY line; then each coming month, with how many items are approaching; then, under no date, anything you keep without a date. The round button with your initials opens the menu: Inbox, Settings and About, the theme colours, ↻ watch the tour and sign out →. The inbox button opens your inbox and shows how many forwarded emails are waiting for you. On most other screens, ← YOUR SKY takes you back home. A household screen opened from Settings shows ← SETTINGS instead. The home screen: the dial with items on it, and below it the list with one overdue item above the TODAY line

sections.title: Add an item
sections.summary: On your home screen, press create. The Add to your orbit drawer opens. Press renewal, service or inspection to start with that type, or something else to choose later.…
sections.text: Add an item On your home screen, press create. The Add to your orbit drawer opens. Press renewal, service or inspection to start with that type, or something else to choose later. You can also press open the full form →. The full form opens. Type a name in Name this entry. Under type, choose one of service, renewal, inspection, suggestion or document (see the next section). Under section, choose where the item belongs. There is no default: you must choose one. Fill in whatever else you know: provider, reference / policy no., key date, recurrence, cost, reminder and notes. These fields appear once you have typed three letters of the name or chosen a type or section. A suggestion has no key date or recurrence; a document has no recurrence. Press Add to orbit. Orbit returns to your home screen with the new item open. Press cancel to leave without saving. Once the rest of the form has opened, Orbit asks Discard this entry? before throwing it away. You can also start from the search box: type a name that matches nothing and choose add "…" as an item. The full form for a renewal named Home contents insurance, with the Home section chosen and provider, reference, key date, recurrence, cost and reminder filled in

sections.title: Choose a type
sections.summary: The type decides what kind of date the item has.
sections.text: Choose a type The type decides what kind of date the item has. Type What it is for Date Repeats service Something done regularly, such as a boiler service optional (needed to repeat) yes renewal Something you renew, such as insurance optional (needed to repeat) yes inspection A check that comes round, such as an MOT optional (needed to repeat) yes document Something that expires once, such as a passport optional no suggestion An idea to keep, with no date no no A document's expiry date is never counted as overdue.

sections.title: Set when it’s due
sections.summary: key date is when the item is next due. recurrence is how often it comes round: one-off, monthly, yearly, or every … months (1 to 120). A new item starts as yearly.
sections.text: Set when it’s due key date is when the item is next due. recurrence is how often it comes round: one-off, monthly, yearly, or every … months (1 to 120). A new item starts as yearly. A repeating item needs a key date. If you choose a repeat without a date, Orbit will not save the item yet; either set the date or choose one-off. Items with no date are kept at the foot of your list under no date and are not drawn on the dial.

sections.title: When Orbit says “not yet”
sections.summary: The Add to orbit button stays unavailable until the item can be saved, and the reason is shown beside it. You may see:
sections.text: When Orbit says “not yet” The Add to orbit button stays unavailable until the item can be saved, and the reason is shown beside it. You may see: not yet — give it a name not yet — choose a section not yet — choose a type not yet — use a dot for pence, for example 12.50 not yet — a repeat needs a due date Nothing you typed is lost while the message shows.

sections.title: Open an item
sections.summary: Press an item on the dial or in the list, and its drawer opens in place. It shows when the item is due, its section, type, orbital period (how often it repeats), cost,…
sections.text: Open an item Press an item on the dial or in the list, and its drawer opens in place. It shows when the item is due, its section, type, orbital period (how often it repeats), cost, provider, reference and reminders, then its notes and documents. Along the bottom are the things you can do: snooze, complete, attach a document and retire. At the right end, the pencil edits the item and the chain-link button copies a link to it. The drawer for Car insurance, showing due date, section, type, orbital period, cost, provider, reference, reminders, one document and the snooze, complete, attach a document and retire buttons

sections.title: Change an item
sections.summary: Open the item and press the pencil (edit). Change what you need. Press due, section, type or orbital period to choose from a list or calendar; type straight into cost,…
sections.text: Change an item Open the item and press the pencil (edit). Change what you need. Press due, section, type or orbital period to choose from a list or calendar; type straight into cost, provider, reference, reminders and notes. Press save. In reminders, type the number of days before the due date for each reminder you want, for example 21 7. Press cancel to stop. If you have changed something, the button first asks discard changes?; press it again to throw the changes away.

sections.title: Mark it done
sections.summary: Open the item and press complete. Check completed on (it starts at today; press it to pick another day). You can also update the cost and notes. If the item repeats,…
sections.text: Mark it done Open the item and press complete. Check completed on (it starts at today; press it to pick another day). You can also update the cost and notes. If the item repeats, Orbit shows then and the next due date. Press record. The next due date counts from the day you say it was done, not from the old due date. An item that does not repeat, or a document, has no next date once completed; its row then says when it was done.

sections.title: Snooze it
sections.summary: Press snooze in the item's drawer and choose a day from the snooze until calendar. The day must be after today. Reminders that would have arrived before that day are not…
sections.text: Snooze it Press snooze in the item's drawer and choose a day from the snooze until calendar. The day must be after today. Reminders that would have arrived before that day are not sent. The due date itself does not change.

sections.title: Retire or restore an item
sections.summary: Press retire, then press again to confirm. The item leaves your list and the dial, but it is not deleted.
sections.text: Retire or restore an item Press retire, then press again to confirm. The item leaves your list and the dial, but it is not deleted. If you open a retired item again, for example from a link you copied, its drawer offers restore to bring it back.

sections.title: Find something
sections.summary: Use the box below the dial on your home screen, explore your world. It matches item names, sections and providers, and the names of attached documents. Use the arrow…
sections.text: Find something Use the box below the dial on your home screen, explore your world. It matches item names, sections and providers, and the names of attached documents. Use the arrow keys to step through the results and Enter to open one.

sections.title: Reminders
sections.summary: Orbit reminds everyone in the household about each item, at 9 in the morning in the household's time zone.
sections.text: Reminders Orbit reminds everyone in the household about each item, at 9 in the morning in the household's time zone. When you add an item, the reminder field lets you pick 1 week before, 2 weeks before or 1 month before; the item then has that one reminder. If you leave it alone, the item takes your first and final warnings instead: 14 days and 3 days before. You can see them under Settings → Reminders, as first warning and final warning; they cannot be changed in the app. To change an item's reminders later, edit the item and change reminders. An item can have up to 8 reminders, each up to 365 days before. Completing an item ends the reminders for that date; a repeating item's reminders start again for its next date. A retired item gets none, and a snoozed item gets none before the day it is snoozed until. Choose how reminders reach you Open Settings and find the Reminders card. email reminders turns reminder emails on or off for you. browser alerts · this device turns alerts on or off in the browser you are using now. Your browser asks for permission the first time. Turn it on in each browser where you want alerts. Both depend on your administrator: outbound mail shows whether email is set up, and browser alerts only work if your administrator has set them up. If both switches are off, Orbit sends you nothing. See what was sent The sent to you lately tab lists recent reminders: which item, which warning, and whether it went by email or browser alert. A reminder that could not be sent says so. Press one to open its item.

sections.title: Documents
sections.summary: Orbit keeps PDFs and photos (JPEG or PNG) with your items. Each file is checked for malware before it is kept, unless your administrator has turned scanning off.
sections.text: Documents Orbit keeps PDFs and photos (JPEG or PNG) with your items. Each file is checked for malware before it is kept, unless your administrator has turned scanning off. Add a document with a new item On the full form, drop a file on drop a document, or press it to choose one. The screen splits: the form on one side and the first page of your document on the other. Nothing is saved until you press Add to orbit; the item and the document are saved together. If your administrator has set up document reading, Orbit reads the file and fills any empty provider, reference / policy no., key date and cost fields with what it found, each marked from document. Check each one: press ✓ accept to confirm it, or type over it. Press not this one to take the file back out; any suggestion you have not accepted goes with it. If Orbit refuses the file, it says why, and the item cannot be added until you drop another file or press remove it to save without one. The create form on the left and page one of a dropped PDF in the reading lane on the right Attach a document to an existing item Open the item and press attach a document, then choose the file. Read a document In an item's drawer, press a document under documents. A preview of the page opens beside the drawer. Press the page to open the reader, where you can turn pages, zoom with −, + and fit, download the file, or close. A file still being checked shows Still scanning this file until it is ready. The Car insurance drawer on the left and a preview of its attached PDF beside it Remove or restore a document Only the person who added a document, the household's owner, or an instance administrator can remove or restore it. In the reader, press remove, then press again to confirm. Orbit keeps a removed document for a while (the preview says until when), and restore puts it back exactly as it was. After that it is gone for good.

sections.title: Forward documents by email
sections.summary: Every member has a private relay address. Forward an email with a document attached to it, and Orbit reads it and puts it in your inbox for review. Nothing is added to…
sections.text: Forward documents by email Every member has a private relay address. Forward an email with a document attached to it, and Orbit reads it and puts it in your inbox for review. Nothing is added to your household until you say so. This only works if your administrator has set up Orbit's mailbox. Set up your relay Open Settings and press open the relay → in the Your relay card. The relay screen shows your address; click it (tap it on a phone) to copy it. If your administrator has paused ingest, the address stays and the screen says collection is paused by the administrator: mail you send now waits and is read when it resumes. Orbit only accepts mail forwarded from the address shown as sending from. If sender check says not yet checked, press send the check email and open the link in that email within 24 hours, while signed in to Orbit. This email needs your administrator to have set up outbound mail. On the same screen: rotate address gives you a new relay address (press twice to confirm); pause ingest stops Orbit collecting your forwarded mail until you press resume ingest. The relay screen with a private address, the sending-from address, sender check marked checked, status, and the rotate address and pause ingest buttons Review what arrived Open your Inbox. Under For your review, each forwarded email shows what Orbit read from it and its attachments. Add to orbit files it as an item, with its documents. Dismiss throws it away. review & amend → opens it on your home screen so you can correct what Orbit read, then add to orbit. Add to orbit and Dismiss each ask you to press twice. If Orbit could not tell the item's type, it says not yet — choose a type in review & amend. Anything left unreviewed burns up after 45 days. Items you have added are listed under Filed. Messages Orbit could not use are listed under Failed to process, with the reason. Forwarded items also appear on your home screen as hollow circles until you decide. Open one to see the same choices. The inbox with one forwarded email for review, a PDF attachment marked scanned clean, and the Add to orbit, Dismiss and review and amend buttons

sections.title: Your household
sections.summary: Open your household's screen by pressing the sun in the middle of your sky, or from Settings → Your systems, which lists every household you belong to.
sections.text: Your household Open your household's screen by pressing the sun in the middle of your sky, or from Settings → Your systems, which lists every household you belong to. Everyone in a household sees its name, time zone and currency, and the Members list. Only the household's owner can change its settings or its members. The household screen as the owner sees it, with the system, sections and members cards Leave a household In Members, press leave this system on your own row, then press again. Everything you added stays with the household. An owner cannot leave or be removed. An owner must hand the household over first. For owners: add people In Members: Add someone who already has an account: press add beside them. Invite by email: type their address and press send invitation. Orbit emails them a link that lasts 14 days. You can resend or withdraw it. This needs your administrator to have set up outbound mail; if not, the invitation shows not sent. Knocking on the door lists people asking to join. Press approve or decline. To remove someone, press remove on their row, then press again. For owners: hand the household over Press hand over → on your row. Choose who takes it, then press hand over to … and press again to confirm. You stay a member and keep everything you added. For owners: sections The Sections card lists the household's sections, up to 12. Rename a section by typing in its name. Use the switch to show or hide a section. A hidden section is not offered when adding an item. Press + add a section to add one. Press × to remove a section. If it still holds items, Orbit asks where they should go. You cannot remove the last section. Press save to keep your changes. For owners: name, time zone and currency In The system, change the name, time zone or currency and press save beside it. The time zone decides what "today" is for the household and when reminders arrive. For owners: take a copy of the household The archive card writes an encrypted file of the household to download. On take it with you, press write an archive →. Choose a passphrase and type it twice. Orbit never keeps it: lose it and the file cannot be opened. Press write the archive, press again, then download the file. The file is kept for a day. Entries and their documents go in the file; people never do. The bring one in tab merges an archive into the household. Entries that are already there stay out. Orbit may first ask for your password, or send you to your identity provider, to confirm it is you. For owners: delete the household Under The danger line, press request deletion →, type the household's name exactly, then press request deletion twice. Everything in the household stops at once. You have 30 days to change your mind: ask your administrator, who can undo it until then.

sections.title: Installing Orbit
sections.summary: How to install Orbit on a Linux machine, what the installer asks, and what it sets up. Once it is running, Running Orbit covers looking after it, and Upgrades and…
sections.text: How to install Orbit on a Linux machine, what the installer asks, and what it sets up. Once it is running, Running Orbit covers looking after it, and Upgrades and backups covers updating and backing up. The installer's guarantees list exactly what each script promises.

sections.title: What you need
sections.summary: A Linux machine with 64-bit x86 processors (amd64). Orbit's builds are made for amd64 only for now. The launcher itself also runs on arm64, but Orbit will not. Docker…
sections.text: What you need A Linux machine with 64-bit x86 processors (amd64). Orbit's builds are made for amd64 only for now. The launcher itself also runs on arm64, but Orbit will not. Docker with Compose v2. curl, openssl, tar, sha256sum and base64, which most Linux systems already have. An HTTPS address for Orbit, served by a reverse proxy on that machine or in front of it. About 4 GiB of free memory for the malware scanner, on top of Orbit and its database. Your reverse proxy must accept uploads a little larger than Orbit's document limit. The limit is 50 MiB by default, and an administrator can change it (up to 100 MiB) with the upload size limit in Administration. Many proxies refuse much smaller requests unless told otherwise, and a document over the proxy's own limit fails with "413" before it reaches Orbit. Set the proxy a little above the limit your administrator chooses: 51 MiB for the default, or 101 MiB to cover every possible setting. Bringing a household in from an Orbit archive that includes documents sends a larger request, up to 343 MiB. If you will import archives, set the proxy to 343 MiB instead; it covers every document setting too. nginx: client_max_body_size 51m; (or 101m;, or 343m;). Its default is 1 MB, so this setting is needed. Caddy: limits request bodies only if you set request_body { max_size 51MiB } (or 101MiB, or 343MiB). Traefik: limits request bodies only if the buffering middleware sets maxRequestBodyBytes (53477376 is 51 MiB; 105906176 is 101 MiB; 359661568 is 343 MiB). If the document limit is raised later, raise the proxy setting to match. Orbit sends its own Content-Security-Policy with every page, which tells the browser where a page may load scripts, images and other content from. If your proxy also sends one, the browser enforces both, and every page goes blank unless the proxy's policy allows everything Orbit's does. That includes inline scripts Orbit marks with a fresh nonce on each page, which a proxy cannot list in advance. So the simplest rule is: send no policy of your own, or one with no script-src (and no default-src) restriction. Do not make the proxy remove Orbit's header. Orbit also refuses to be shown inside another site's frame: every response carries X-Frame-Options: DENY, and the policy on every page the server draws says frame-ancestors 'none'. The three sign-in pages built ahead of time (/login, /logout, /auth/error) carry their policy in the page itself, where frame-ancestors has no effect, so the X-Frame-Options header covers them. A proxy need not add either.

sections.title: What runs where
sections.summary: Orbit runs as a few Docker containers on one machine. Your browser talks only to the Orbit container, usually through your reverse proxy. The database and the other…
sections.text: What runs where Orbit runs as a few Docker containers on one machine. Your browser talks only to the Orbit container, usually through your reverse proxy. The database and the other helpers cannot be reached from the browser. flowchart LR user["Browser or installed app"] proxy["Your reverse proxy"] orbit["orbit (the app and its background work)"] db[("orbit-postgres: database")] files[("Document volume, encrypted")] clamav["orbit-clamav: malware scanner"] tika["orbit-tika (optional): document text reader"] ollama["orbit-ollama (optional): private AI model server"] mail["Your mail servers (IMAP and SMTP)"] push["Browser push services"] oidc["Your identity provider (optional)"] user <-->|HTTPS| proxy proxy <-->|"port 3000"| orbit orbit <--> db orbit --> files orbit --> clamav orbit --> tika orbit --> ollama orbit <--> mail orbit --> push orbit <-.-> oidc Container What it does When it runs orbit Orbit itself: the web app, plus the background work that sends reminders, processes documents and collects mail. Always. orbit-postgres The database (PostgreSQL 18). Always. orbit-clamav The malware scanner. Uploads are scanned before they are kept. Always. orbit-tika Reads the text in documents so Orbit can suggest an item's details. Only with the Document processing or Full local stack profile. orbit-ollama A private AI model server on your own machine. Only with the Full local stack profile, or Custom, Local Ollama infrastructure only. Things worth knowing: Orbit listens on port 3000 by default. ORBIT_PORT changes the port and ORBIT_BIND_ADDRESS chooses which network address it listens on; see Open Orbit. Your documents are kept encrypted in one Docker volume, and the database is in another. A backup covers both: see Upgrades and backups. The scanner, the text reader and the model server share a private network with Orbit. Of the three, only the scanner has a separate connection out, which it uses to update its malware signatures. None of them can reach the database. Orbit itself connects out to the mail servers you set up, to browser push services when people turn on alerts, and to your identity provider if you use one.

sections.title: Install
sections.summary: From an empty directory, run:
sections.text: Install From an empty directory, run: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tomlawesome/orbit/main/scripts/get-orbit.sh | bash This one line downloads and checks the signed Orbit launcher before it runs anything: it checks the release's signed manifest (the list of files that make up the release) against Orbit's public key; if cosign is installed, it also checks a second, independent signature, and refuses if that signature is missing; it checks every file it downloads against the checksum in the manifest. Only once everything checks out does it start the launcher, which runs the installer described below. It installs the newest stable release. To install one particular release instead, put ORBIT_VERSION=v0.3.0 (or another version) in front of bash. Installer guarantees says exactly what is checked (its get-orbit.sh section), and Releasing says how the signatures are made. Git is not needed and nothing is cloned. A deployment needs only the Compose files, a few operator scripts and a published build of Orbit, not the source code. What the installer asks The installer shows a menu: Install, Update, Repair or Exit. Install sets up a new Orbit in an empty directory. It first asks which profile you want: Standard (Orbit, its database and the malware scanner), Document processing (adds a local document text reader), Full local stack (adds a private AI model server as well), or Custom. It then asks whether people will sign in with Orbit's own accounts only (the default) or also through an identity provider, an external sign-in service such as Authentik. With Orbit's own accounts, it needs only Orbit's public address. With an identity provider, it also needs the provider's address (the "issuer"), the client ID the provider gave you, and the client secret, which you type hidden. Nothing in the directory changes until you accept the final review screen. Update moves an existing Orbit to the new release. If the current settings are complete, it keeps them and your secrets as they are and does not ask for them again. From a terminal, it asks whether to keep the current profile, then shows a review screen before it changes anything. Back up first: see Upgrades and backups. Repair changes nothing. It tells you to run bash scripts/repair.sh --check to find what is wrong, then --plan to see what a repair would do. When everything is running, the last screen shows Orbit's address, the version, the exact build installed, the profile, and the commands for status and logs. It then tells you two things to do next: Claim the new Orbit: the link that creates its first administrator is printed in the Orbit container's log. See Claiming a fresh install. Export a recovery bundle, the only way back in if the document encryption key is ever lost. See Exporting a recovery bundle. What gets installed The installer downloads Orbit from the release registry and records exactly which build it downloaded, using the build's digest: a fingerprint that identifies one build and nothing else. That fingerprint is written to .env-orbit, and that build is what runs, so nothing can swap in a different build behind your back. The Compose files and operator scripts come out of that same build, so they always match the version they came with. The directory ends up holding docker-compose.yml, the extra Compose files docker-compose.mail.yml, docker-compose.kek-rotation.yml and docker-compose.no-document-key.yml, .env-orbit.example, config/tika-config.json, the scripts configure.sh, backup.sh, restore.sh, repair.sh, export-recovery-bundle.sh, import-recovery-bundle.sh, end-maintenance.sh and installer-ui.sh, your settings in .env-orbit, and your secrets in .orbit-secrets/. The installer itself only fetches, checks and starts things. Everything that reads or writes the directory — checking it is safe to install into, asking your questions, writing the settings and secrets, and checking your sign-in provider — runs inside that same build, in a short-lived container that is removed when it finishes. If anything goes wrong before Orbit starts, it puts the directory back exactly as it was. The installer then generates four separate secrets: one for sign-in sessions, the database password, the document encryption key, and the private key for browser alerts. They live in .orbit-secrets/, readable only by the user who ran the installer. Each container is given only the secret files it needs; secret values never go into container environment variables. Later runs keep the secrets you already have. It reports success only once the database is healthy, Orbit's own health check at /api/health says ready, the malware scanner is healthy, and each optional service you chose answers its check. If you cancel during the questions, or a run finds a setting that needs attention, the installer puts its files back as they were and prints only the names of the settings and what to do next. Run the install line again, or fix the settings directly from the deployment directory: bash scripts/configure.sh --init bash scripts/configure.sh --set-oidc-secret bash scripts/configure.sh --check These commands run inside the Orbit image, so Docker must be running and the image must be available, even for a one-line change. configure.sh takes the image from ORBIT_IMAGE in your environment, or else from the ORBIT_IMAGE= line the installer wrote to .env-orbit. If it finds neither it stops with: Orbit configuration: No Orbit image to run configuration with. Set ORBIT_IMAGE to an immutable registry digest (or the local tag scripts/build-container.sh builds), or install with get-orbit.sh, which records it in .env-orbit. To go on, set ORBIT_IMAGE to the build's registry digest and run the command again. A digest that is not on this machine yet is pulled first. Files configure.sh creates belong to the user who ran it. If an install fails When a new install fails after it has started writing files, the installer puts the directory back as it found it and removes the containers and volumes it created. It deletes only the files it wrote itself: anything else new in the directory, such as a note you saved there while it ran, is moved into orbit-install-backups/<date and time>/moved/, and the installer prints where. One exception: .env-orbit and .orbit-secrets/ are put back whole from the copy taken at the start, so an edit or a file added inside them while the install ran is replaced, and the closing line says so when the rollback finishes. If it could not stop the containers, it keeps the files it wrote in that dated folder's engine/ instead, and prints one command to stop them; run it, then install again. orbit-install-backups/ is not a backup of your Orbit data (that is what scripts/backup.sh makes). It is readable only by you; the installer never reads, runs, moves or deletes anything in a folder from an earlier run, and later installs ignore it. A run removes only its own copy of your original files once they are put back, and its own dated folder when that leaves it empty. You can leave it there. If an update stops An update that stops after it has written its files is not undone: run the update again and it carries on from there. If it stopped before the containers were replaced and was made by an installer older than this release, the next run may refuse because the running build differs from ORBIT_IMAGE. Then start the deployment again from its folder, and run the update again.

sections.title: Logged and unattended runs
sections.summary: The options in this section belong to install.sh, the installer script the launcher runs for you. Running install.sh on its own is not a supported way to install (see…
sections.text: Logged and unattended runs The options in this section belong to install.sh, the installer script the launcher runs for you. Running install.sh on its own is not a supported way to install (see Releasing); the options are listed for automated and test runs. Add --plain for output with no screen drawing, one line at a time, safe for logs and pipes. Name the action with --install, --update or --repair; with none, it installs into an empty directory and updates a directory that already holds Orbit. --install accepts only an empty directory (or a prepared one, below); --update accepts only a directory that already holds Orbit. --simulate (with --plain if you like) is a rehearsal. It shows the same menus, questions and example success and failure screens, using clearly labelled made-up values. It does not read or change the directory, and it never contacts Docker, a registry or an identity provider. It cannot be combined with --install, --update or --repair. Installing with no questions For an unattended install, the directory must already hold a complete .env-orbit and, optionally, an .orbit-secrets/ directory, and nothing else. Before it downloads anything, the installer checks that: .env-orbit is a plain file (not a symlink) with permissions 0600; .orbit-secrets/, if it is there, is a real directory (not a symlink) with permissions 0700, and every file inside it is a plain, non-empty file with permissions 0600; if .env-orbit sets ORBIT_AUTH_OIDC=true (people sign in through an identity provider), .orbit-secrets/oidc-client-secret exists. With Orbit's own accounts only, .env-orbit on its own is enough: the installer creates .orbit-secrets/ and generates the other secrets. The exception is an .env-orbit that still names OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE (kept when SSO is switched off): then the secret file must be there too, or the install stops and changes nothing; .env-orbit passes bash scripts/configure.sh --check. Anything else is refused before Docker or any download starts: extra files, symlinks, empty files, looser permissions, a setting that still needs attention, an invalid callback address, or an optional group of settings that is only half filled in. If the configuration check, the identity provider lookup or the Compose check then fails, your files are left exactly as they were.

sections.title: Running Orbit
sections.summary: How to look after an Orbit once it is installed: opening it, starting and stopping it, changing its settings, the optional document services, and where to find updates…
sections.text: How to look after an Orbit once it is installed: opening it, starting and stopping it, changing its settings, the optional document services, and where to find updates and backups. Run every command on this page from the deployment directory, the one you installed into. Installing Orbit lists what that directory holds.

sections.title: Open Orbit
sections.summary: Open the address in APP_URL. For a real deployment that is an HTTPS address, and your reverse proxy must pass it on to Orbit's port, 3000 by default (ORBIT_PORT). Plain…
sections.text: Open Orbit Open the address in APP_URL. For a real deployment that is an HTTPS address, and your reverse proxy must pass it on to Orbit's port, 3000 by default (ORBIT_PORT). Plain HTTP works only on the machine itself, at http://127.0.0.1:3000. Orbit's health check is at /api/health. By default Orbit listens on every network interface of the machine. Set ORBIT_BIND_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1 in .env-orbit when only the machine itself, or a reverse proxy running on it, should reach Orbit. Never open port 3000 directly to the internet. [!IMPORTANT] Use one address everywhere: APP_URL, the address in the browser, and the callback address registered with an identity provider. Do not switch between localhost and 127.0.0.1 part-way through a sign-in.

sections.title: Claim it and create your household
sections.summary: Nobody sees a household without signing in. A new Orbit stays unclaimed until someone opens the claim link Orbit prints in its log:
sections.text: Claim it and create your household Nobody sees a household without signing in. A new Orbit stays unclaimed until someone opens the claim link Orbit prints in its log: docker compose --env-file .env-orbit logs orbit-app That person becomes the first instance administrator. Claiming a fresh install has the detail, including who else could read that link. Next, Orbit shows the "where do you belong?" card. On a new install there is nothing to ask to join, so the card's "name your own system" drawer is already open. (If other households exist, they are listed with "ask to join", and you open the drawer with "name your own system".) The drawer asks for three things to create the first household: its name, its time zone and its currency. It starts every household with four sections, Home, Vehicles, Devices and Services, which you can rename, reorder, recolour or add to later on the household screen. The create form in the belong card's drawer: a name, a time zone and a currency, with a note that four sections come to start Instance administrators can see every household and add any person to any household. The People card in Administration shows each person as "admin" or "user", but it has no control yet to give or remove administrator access (issue #1633).

sections.title: Start, stop and check on it
sections.summary: The first two show what is running and its recent log, and are the commands the installer prints at the end. up -d starts everything in the background, and stop stops it…
sections.text: Start, stop and check on it docker compose --env-file .env-orbit ps docker compose --env-file .env-orbit logs --tail 200 docker compose --env-file .env-orbit up -d docker compose --env-file .env-orbit stop The first two show what is running and its recent log, and are the commands the installer prints at the end. up -d starts everything in the background, and stop stops it without removing anything. Keep using --env-file .env-orbit from the deployment directory, with no --project-name, so every command finds the same containers and data. On start, Orbit waits for its database, applies any pending database updates (migrations), starts its reminder scheduler, then opens for visitors.

sections.title: Change the settings
sections.summary: Every setting lives in .env-orbit and is listed in Configuration. After an edit, check the file, then start Orbit again so it reads the change:
sections.text: Change the settings Every setting lives in .env-orbit and is listed in Configuration. After an edit, check the file, then start Orbit again so it reads the change: bash scripts/configure.sh --check docker compose --env-file .env-orbit up -d --check prints each setting's name and whether it is ready, never its value. Three more commands help: bash scripts/configure.sh --init asks again how people sign in: Orbit's own accounts only, or an identity provider as well, and if so the provider's details. bash scripts/configure.sh --set-oidc-secret stores the identity provider's client secret, typed hidden, in .orbit-secrets/. bash scripts/configure.sh on its own fills in any setting or secret that is missing and leaves the rest alone. All of these run inside the Orbit image: configure.sh starts a short-lived container from it, with no network, and that container reads and writes the files. Docker must therefore be running and the image must be available, even to change one setting. The image comes from ORBIT_IMAGE in your environment, or else from the ORBIT_IMAGE= line in .env-orbit, which the installer writes. With neither, it stops with: Orbit configuration: No Orbit image to run configuration with. Set ORBIT_IMAGE to an immutable registry digest (or the local tag scripts/build-container.sh builds), or install with get-orbit.sh, which records it in .env-orbit. Set ORBIT_IMAGE to the build's registry digest (on a source checkout, the local tag scripts/build-container.sh builds) and run it again. A digest that is not on this machine is pulled first; a local tag that is not on this machine is refused, because there is nothing to pull. Files it creates belong to the user who ran it. Deployment configuration readiness explains each of these in full, and Authentication covers identity providers.

sections.title: Optional document services
sections.summary: The standard set-up already checks every upload for malware. Two more services are optional, because they need a lot of memory and Orbit works without them:
sections.text: Optional document services The standard set-up already checks every upload for malware. Two more services are optional, because they need a lot of memory and Orbit works without them: Apache Tika, a document text reader. With it, Orbit reads the text of uploaded and forwarded documents so it can suggest an item's details. It does not read text out of scanned images: that feature (OCR) is switched off. Ollama, a private AI model server. With a model chosen, Orbit also asks the model to suggest a document's provider, reference, type, cost, how often it recurs and its dates, and checks the answer against its own rules. Either way, nothing is added until you review it. To turn both on, add these lines to .env-orbit: TIKA_URL=http://orbit-tika:9998 # Choose a local model only after checking its size, licence and memory needs. OLLAMA_MODEL=<a-local-model-name> COMPOSE_PROFILES=processing,ai processing turns on Tika and ai turns on Ollama; leave COMPOSE_PROFILES empty to run neither. Then start Orbit as usual with docker compose --env-file .env-orbit up -d. To turn them off again, empty COMPOSE_PROFILES, then stop and remove the two containers. Downloaded models stay in their volume: docker compose --env-file .env-orbit --profile processing --profile ai \ rm --stop --force orbit-tika orbit-ollama Neither service can be reached from outside the machine, and neither can reach the internet or the database. Ollama is limited to 2 CPUs and 6 GiB of memory by default, and Tika to 1 GiB. Because Ollama cannot reach the internet, it cannot download a model itself. Set OLLAMA_MODEL first, then run the one-off helper, which downloads the model and exits: docker compose --env-file .env-orbit --profile ai-model-pull \ run --rm orbit-ollama-model-pull Private model server and its model pull has the detail, including machines with no internet access.

sections.title: Before the first real use
sections.summary: Open Orbit at its HTTPS address and sign in, with Orbit's own accounts or your identity provider. Set up email. Password sign-ins are approved by an emailed link (see…
sections.text: Before the first real use Open Orbit at its HTTPS address and sign in, with Orbit's own accounts or your identity provider. Set up email. Password sign-ins are approved by an emailed link (see Authentication), and reminders go by email too. The administration screen's provider tests check the connection. Schedule bash scripts/backup.sh, keep copies off this machine, and try a restore. Upgrades and backups shows how to back up, check and restore. Export a recovery bundle and store it, and its passphrase, away from this machine. Read Encryption at rest and decide whether the machine's disk needs encrypting. Orbit does not decide this for you.

sections.title: Upgrades and backups
sections.summary: How to update Orbit, how to back it up, and how to go back if an update goes wrong. Run every command on this page from the deployment directory, the one you installed…
sections.text: How to update Orbit, how to back it up, and how to go back if an update goes wrong. Run every command on this page from the deployment directory, the one you installed into. The short version: back up, check the backup, update, and check that Orbit is healthy and you can sign in. Keep the backup until you are sure.

sections.title: Back up
sections.summary: This makes one file in backups/, named like orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar, and prints Orbit backup created: followed by its path. The file holds a copy of the database and…
sections.text: Back up bash scripts/backup.sh This makes one file in backups/, named like orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar, and prints Orbit backup created: followed by its path. The file holds a copy of the database and an encrypted copy of the stored documents. Orbit is stopped while the backup runs, so the copy is of one moment in time, and is started again afterwards. To keep backups somewhere else, set ORBIT_BACKUP_DIR to that directory when you run the script. If you set it, set it the same way for every backup, restore, --recover and --finish: a restore keeps its recovery record in that directory. The host needs Docker with Compose v2. Orbit's document key file, .orbit-secrets/document-kek, must be in place. A backup does not hold your settings (.env-orbit) or your secrets. Check a backup at any time with: bash scripts/backup.sh --verify backups/orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar This reads the file and changes nothing, and Orbit keeps running. A backup needs the document key A backup is tied to the document encryption key it was made with, so it is only useful on a machine that still has that key. To be able to recover after losing the machine, also export a recovery bundle, protected by a passphrase, and keep it somewhere else. See Exporting a recovery bundle. Backups, restores and updates are refused while a document key rotation is open. See Rotating the document key-encryption key.

subs.title: A backup needs the document key

sections.title: Update
sections.summary: Back up, and check the backup, as above. Keep a copy of your settings next to it, in the same directory as the backup (backups, or your ORBIT_BACKUP_DIR). The copy…
sections.text: Update Back up, and check the backup, as above. Keep a copy of your settings next to it, in the same directory as the backup (backups, or your ORBIT_BACKUP_DIR). The copy records exactly which build was running, so you can go back to it: umask 077 mkdir -p backups cp .env-orbit backups/orbit-pre-upgrade.env Run the install line from Installing Orbit again, in the deployment directory, and choose Update. If it stops part-way, run the update again; see If an update stops. Afterwards, open Orbit, check /api/health, and sign in. Keep using docker compose --env-file .env-orbit from the deployment directory, with no --project-name, so every command finds the same containers and data. Update from no more than three releases back An install can update directly only from the last three stable releases before the one you are installing; retracted releases do not count. From further back, the installer stops before it pulls or changes anything and names the release to update to first, for example This install is on v0.3.1. Update to v0.3.4 first, then to v0.3.6. To step through, install the release it names (pin it with its version tag, for example ORBIT_VERSION=v0.3.4, as in Installing Orbit), check /api/health, then run the update again for the next release. Each stop repeats the check, so a long way back takes a few steps. An install whose .env-orbit records an applied digest (ORBIT_CONFIG_APPLIED_DIGEST) but no ORBIT_CONFIG_APPLIED_VERSION, or is on a version that is not a stable release, is refused with a line saying so (an env file with neither is a fresh install); run bash scripts/repair.sh --check first.

subs.title: Update from no more than three releases back

sections.title: Go back after a failed update
sections.summary: If Orbit has started on the new build but the database update or sign-in then fails, stop it and restore both the backup and the saved settings:
sections.text: Go back after a failed update If Orbit has started on the new build but the database update or sign-in then fails, stop it and restore both the backup and the saved settings: docker compose --env-file .env-orbit stop orbit-app cp backups/orbit-pre-upgrade.env .env-orbit chmod 600 .env-orbit docker compose --env-file .env-orbit pull orbit-app bash scripts/restore.sh backups/orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar Use the backup you made in step 1 of the update. The saved .env-orbit names the previous build exactly, so do not swap in a version name or edit only ORBIT_IMAGE. Type RESTORE when it asks. Then check /api/health, check that you can sign in on the previous build, and only then delete the saved copy: rm -f backups/orbit-pre-upgrade.env Installer guarantees lists exactly what the installer promises around an upgrade.

sections.title: Restore
sections.summary: The restore checks the backup, stops Orbit, checks the backup again, and asks you to type RESTORE. If you do not, Orbit starts again unchanged. Once you do, it takes a…
sections.text: Restore bash scripts/restore.sh backups/orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar The restore checks the backup, stops Orbit, checks the backup again, and asks you to type RESTORE. If you do not, Orbit starts again unchanged. Once you do, it takes a recovery checkpoint, replaces the database and the stored documents with the ones in the backup, starts Orbit and waits for it to answer. On a new machine, or any machine without the original document key, first put the key back from your recovery bundle: see Restoring the document key-encryption key. Then run the restore. If a restore is interrupted part-way, or Orbit is not healthy afterwards, Orbit stays stopped and bash scripts/restore.sh --recover puts the previous state back. If Orbit is running the restored data but the restore says it could not finish, run bash scripts/restore.sh --finish. Until a restore is finished or recovered, new backups and restores are refused. Both scripts run Orbit's engine inside the deployment, so the host needs Docker with Compose v2. Restore also needs curl, to wait for Orbit to answer; backup does not. An unattended restore skips the typed RESTORE only when given both switches, so that neither alone can replace your data: ORBIT_NONINTERACTIVE_RESTORE=true bash scripts/restore.sh --yes backups/orbit-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar --yes without the variable stops before Orbit is touched.

sections.title: What it is
sections.summary: orbit-launcher is the full-screen terminal program that installs, updates, repairs and removes Orbit on the server that hosts it. Orbit's install line downloads it,…
sections.text: What it is orbit-launcher is the full-screen terminal program that installs, updates, repairs and removes Orbit on the server that hosts it. Orbit's install line downloads it, checks it and starts it for you.

sections.title: What you need
sections.summary: A Linux server. Orbit's download script stops on any other system, and on anything but 64-bit x86 or arm64. Orbit itself is built for 64-bit x86 (amd64) only for now, so…
sections.text: What you need A Linux server. Orbit's download script stops on any other system, and on anything but 64-bit x86 or arm64. Orbit itself is built for 64-bit x86 (amd64) only for now, so use amd64. The launcher is tested by installing Orbit on Ubuntu and on Fedora. Docker with Compose v2. Plus curl, openssl, tar, sha256sum, base64 and GNU timeout, which most Linux systems already have. A normal user account that can use Docker. The launcher refuses to run as root, with or without sudo. Memory. The launcher counts 6 GiB for Standard: Orbit's 2 GiB and the malware scanner's 4 GiB memory limits. The database and the system need memory on top of that. Documents adds a 1 GiB attachment reader, 7 GiB in all. The launcher reads the machine's total memory on Linux and will not start Documents when it is under 7 GiB. It never blocks Standard. Ports. Orbit listens on port 3000 on every network interface unless you change ORBIT_PORT or ORBIT_BIND_ADDRESS in .env-orbit. Put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of it. Never expose Orbit directly to the internet. Installing Orbit covers the proxy. Disk. No minimum is documented. If Orbit fails to start, the installer reports the free space on the install folder and on Docker's data folder. Internet access to GitHub (the install files and the launcher's update check), to GitHub's container registry (ghcr.io, for Orbit's image) and to Docker Hub (for the database, scanner and attachment-reader images). While Orbit runs, the scanner also downloads its signature updates. Set ORBIT_LAUNCHER_NO_UPDATE_CHECK to any non-empty value to skip the launcher's update check.

sections.title: Install, then claim
sections.summary: The short version. Installing Orbit has the full requirements and explains the sign-in questions. Its menu and profile names are those of Orbit's plain installer, not…
sections.text: Install, then claim The short version. Installing Orbit has the full requirements and explains the sign-in questions. Its menu and profile names are those of Orbit's plain installer, not the launcher's. Set up the HTTPS reverse proxy for Orbit's public address first (Installing Orbit covers its settings). The claim link opens that address, so it must already reach Orbit on port 3000. Make an empty folder for Orbit and open a terminal in it. The launcher works on the folder it is started from. Run the install line from Installing Orbit. It checks the signed release and starts the launcher. Choose Install, then a profile: Standard or Documents. The Agent and Full rows show "not yet". Read the note about Orbit's state and risks. After a 20-second countdown, and once you have scrolled to the end, type I've read this and I understand to go on. Watch the install run in the launcher's console. Orbit then asks for its settings (its public address, how people sign in) in that console, or briefly hands you the terminal to answer. On the final screen, the address shows as alive and unclaimed. Choose Get into Orbit to open the claim link, or Copy claim link if the server has no browser (your terminal must allow clipboard writes). Whoever opens the link first creates the first administrator, so open it yourself. If no link shows, run docker compose --env-file .env-orbit logs orbit-app in the folder and open the link Orbit printed. After that, export a recovery bundle, as Installing Orbit explains.

sections.title: Update and Repair
sections.summary: Run the install line again from the Orbit folder and choose:
sections.text: Update and Repair Run the install line again from the Orbit folder and choose: Update pulls the latest Orbit and updates this deployment, keeping its configuration. The launcher takes no backup, and Orbit's note says an upgrade may not keep your data, so back up first (see the link at the end). One-step update with a backup, a health check and rollback is planned (issue #317 in the launcher's GitLab project, update in one step). Repair runs the deployment's own scripts/repair.sh to diagnose it and shows what a fix would do. It changes nothing until you agree, and offers only the actions the plan proposes. It cannot yet start services that failed to start: issue #256 in the launcher's GitLab project.

sections.title: What Remove deletes
sections.summary: Remove works in two steps, and the launcher runs only the first.
sections.text: What Remove deletes Remove works in two steps, and the launcher runs only the first. Stand down (the launcher runs this after you confirm). It runs docker compose down: it stops Orbit and removes its containers and network. It deletes no files, no data volumes and no images. The removal command (you decide whether to run it). The launcher shows a command and offers to copy it, but never runs it. It is docker compose … down -v && sudo rm -rf <your Orbit folder>. It deletes the data volumes (the database, with its mail, and the documents and scanner volumes) and the whole folder: configuration, secrets, backups and anything else you put there. It cannot be undone. It leaves Docker images alone. If the folder is the root folder or your home folder, the launcher offers only the data-volume half and leaves the folder for you. Removing the data volumes matters: a database volume left behind makes a later install stop. Remove acts only on the Orbit found in the folder you start the launcher in. A change so that Remove deletes only Orbit's own files, and keeps everything else in the folder, is planned: issue #285 in the launcher's GitLab project.

sections.text: Options orbit-launcher --version prints its version. orbit-launcher --licences prints the licences of what it includes. ORBIT_LAUNCHER_NO_ANIMATION, set to any non-empty value, skips the opening animation.
